BV","content-domain":{"domain":[],"crossmark-restriction":false},"abstract":"<jats:p>We live in a republic of amended statutes. In each Congress, our laws are amended tens of thousands of times. Individual statutes make amendments that number in the thousands. As a result, the amended statute has become the central democratic text of our age\u2014a remarkable development for a type of document unknown at the Founding. Yet the amended statute has been relegated to an afterthought in legal theory. This is incredible neglect for an essential source of modern law\u2014one that anchors innumerable rights in U.S. society.&nbsp;<br><br>This Article demonstrates that, instead, the amended statute belongs at the center of public law. To that end, it undertakes three projects with respect to the amended statute: documenting, theorizing, and interpreting.&nbsp;<br><br>It begins with documenting. Through a study consisting of over seven hundred searches of the Statutes at Large, it identifies\u2014for the first time\u2014the nearly half-million amendments made to federal statutes since the Founding. In so doing, it tells the story of statutory amendments in U.S. law. It is a story of remarkable transformation: from a statutory corpus with no amendments through the 1830s to one that now undergoes over eight thousand amendments each year. Contemporary statutes, it reveals, typically are amended statutes.&nbsp;<br><br>Next, the Article theorizes amended statutory law. Despite its neglect in current legal theory, the amended statute was transformative. It created a new idea of the \"statute\" in the United States\u2014introducing a new document, and one with different traits than the traditional statute. The Article theorizes the key changes this introduced into: (1) legislation, (2) the legislative process, (3) the institution of the legislature, and (4) statutory interpretation. These changes include enabling the rise of textualism, making methodological originalism impossible in interpretation, and divorcing the drafter from the legislator. The Article chronicles these many theoretical insights.&nbsp;<br><br>Finally, the Article asks how to interpret amended statutory law. Revisiting two recent classics of statutory interpretation, <i>Niz-Chavez v. Garland<\/i> and <i>Van Buren v. United States<\/i>, it uncovers the unknown amendatory stories behind these landmark cases. In so doing, it shows the contemporary Supreme Court's troubling inability to locate democratic decisions beneath the amended statute. And it models a competing method of interpretation\u2014one more appropriate for a republic of amended statutes.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.5426276","type":"posted-content","created":{"date-parts":[[2025,9,2]],"date-time":"2025-09-02T20:13:40Z","timestamp":1756844020000},"source":"Crossref","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["The Amended Statute"],"prefix":"10.2139","author":[{"given":"Jesse","family":"Cross","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"member":"78","reference":[{"key":"ref1","author":"William N See","year":"1994","journal-title":"DYNAMIC STATUTORY INTERPRETATION 126-28"},{"key":"ref2","first-page":"1519","author":"N William","year":"1987","journal-title":"Dynamic Statutory Interpretation"},{"key":"ref3","first-page":"228","author":"Ronald Dworkin","year":"1986"},{"key":"ref4","first-page":"540","article-title":"Law as Interpretation, 60 TEX","volume":"527","author":"Ronald Dworkin","year":"1982","journal-title":"L. Neither hybrid scoring nor cross-encoder reranking improved over pure BM25. BV","content-domain":{"domain":[],"crossmark-restriction":false},"abstract":"<jats:p>Legal judgment prediction (LJP) using large language models (LLMs) is increasingly explored; however, its practical deployment remains constrained by hallucinations and limited evidentiary traceability, challenges that are especially acute in under\u2011resourced, statute\u2011centric Arabic legal systems. This paper introduces ArabLJP, an evidence\u2011grounded and retrieval\u2011augmented framework that reframes Arabic LJP as statute\u2011conditioned judgment generation rather than label\u2011only classification. ArabLJP integrates (i) a reasoning-preserving Saudi commercial\u2011law dataset that explicitly retains factual narratives, judicial reasoning, and operative rulings; (ii) a hybrid \"Smart RAG\" retrieval pipeline that combines lexical matching, semantic embeddings, and LLM\u2011guided query refinement and reranking, with priority grounding in statutes explicitly cited in case materials; and (iii) a hallucination\u2011aware, multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that measures semantic alignment, entity and numeric consistency, and outcome fidelity, with explicit penalties for unsupported factual inventions. The framework is evaluated under controlled experimental conditions across three modeling paradigms: prompt\u2011only generation; retrieval\u2011augmented structured prompting; and parameter\u2011efficient supervised adaptation, and multiple LLM backbones, including gpt\u201140\u2011mini and four open\u2011weight models (LLaMA\u20113.2, Qwen\u20113, Phi\u20114, and DeepSeek). Empirical results demonstrate that evidence\u2011grounded retrieval and structured prompting substantially reduce hallucination strength and improve ruling fidelity relative to prompt-only baselines, while supervised adaptation yields further gains in semantic and stylistic alignment with reference judgments. Overall, ArabLJP shows that disciplined statutory grounding, structured judicial prompting, and reliability-oriented evaluation measurably improve LJP robustness in Arabic, statute\u2011centric legal settings. The framework provides a reproducible methodological baseline for studying and mitigating hallucinations in Arabic LJP, while underscoring that fully reliable automated legal reasoning remains an open
